sections.text:
This part of the Blog will go through the code and logic used to create 'The Long Way Round'.

The Godot game engine uses its own Language GDScript, which is syntactically similar to Python.

Example code snippet:

images.caption: Example GDScript code
Start Menu Sketch.

The start menu takes strong inspiration from PlayStation 1 era games like Silent Hill and Tekken. I was particularly interested in their minimal design approach, where menus are stripped back to just the essentials, typically the game title and basic options like start and quit. I chose to follow this style to keep the interface simple, readable, and nostalgic, while also ensuring the player can navigate it quickly and intuitively.
Start Menu Final w/o easy mode secret option:
Start Menu Code:

Code breakdown:

This script controls the functionality of the game’s start menu using GDScript, attached to a Control node in the Godot engine.

When the scene loads, the _ready() function connects button signals (such as pressed and mouse_entered) to custom handler functions, allowing the menu to respond to user interaction.

When the Start button is clicked, a click sound effect is played and a “flash” animation is triggered via the AnimationPlayer.

The script then waits for the animation to finish using await, ensuring a smooth transition before changing to the intro scene with SceneTransition.change_scene(). If the Quit button is pressed, a sound plays and the game closes using get_tree().quit(). Additionally, hovering over either button triggers a hover sound effect, providing audio feedback and improving the user experience.

The intro scene is based on Embassy Gardens. Before designing the final background, I used a stock image of the area as a stand-in during development.The Embassy Gardens building was actually a massive inspiration behind the project (which i go into more detail in the misc part of the blog).

This is where the visual novel style comes into play. I chose a minimal text box design, loosely inspired by Undertale, featuring a classic black-and-white aesthetic for clarity and readability.

This script manages a simple dialogue system in Godot. It cycles through lines of text stored in an array and displays them using a typewriter effect. When the scene starts, the first line is shown, and each line is revealed gradually while playing a sound effect.

This part of the script controls how the dialogue is displayed and how the player interacts with it. The type_text() function is responsible for creating the typewriter effect. It loops through each character in the current line of dialogue (full_text) and gradually builds the visible text by adding one character at a time to current_text. After each character is added, the label is updated and the script waits briefly using await and a timer, which creates the animated typing effect.

While the text is being revealed, the script checks whether is_typing is still true. If it has been set to false, the function immediately stops typing and also stops the dialogue sound. Once the entire line has been displayed, is_typing is set to false, a hint is made visible to prompt the player, and the sound effect is stopped.

The _input(event) function handles player interaction. It listens for either a keyboard input (such as pressing the key mapped to ui_accept) or a mouse click. If the player provides input while the text is still typing, the typing effect is skipped and the full line of dialogue is instantly displayed. The sound effect is stopped and the hint becomes visible. If the player presses input after the line has finished displaying, the script moves on to the next line by calling next_line

The next_line() function advances the dialogue by increasing the dialogue_index. If there are still lines remaining in the dialogue array, it calls show_line() to display the next one. If all lines have been shown, the script stops the dialogue sound and transitions to a new scene using SceneTransition.change_scene()
Outside background sketch.
In game presentation.

I initially used a free office background as a placeholder to better approximate the final look of the scene. This also helped me experiment with the placement of the character and text box, as well as understand how much of the background would be obscured during gameplay.

Concierge screen grab. The background was illustrated by a friend and fellow artist, Calix Borrero-Diaz. The colours were slightly desaturated to help the character stand out more clearly. The overall colour palette is intentionally brighter to create a strong contrast with the ‘Poor Door’ entrance area.

This section sets up the core of the dialogue system. The script extends a Control node, meaning it manages UI elements like the text box. The dialogue array stores each line as an object with both text and a type (player, NPC, or description), allowing different speakers to be styled differently.

The remaining variables control how the dialogue is displayed. dialogue_index tracks the current line, while full_text and current_text are used to create the typewriter effect. is_typing determines whether the text is still appearing, and typing_speed controls how fast it displays. current_color changes the text colour based on the speaker, and using_sound2 is used to switch between different sound effects during certain lines.

This part of the script handles the setup and display of each dialogue line. When the scene starts, the ready function hides the hint and character, sets the character animation to idle, and enables BBCode on the dialogue label so coloured text can be used. It then begins the dialogue sequence.

The start function resets the dialogue index and calls the function responsible for showing the current line. The show_line function reads the current entry from the dialogue array and checks the speaker type. Based on whether the line is narration, player dialogue, or NPC dialogue, it assigns a different text colour to visually distinguish who is speaking.

It then prepares the text for display by storing the full line, clearing the current visible text, and enabling the typing effect. The dialogue label is cleared, the hint is hidden, and sound settings are reset so the next line can be displayed cleanly.

This section controls the audio and character behaviour for each line of dialogue. At the start, both sound effects are stopped to ensure there is no overlap from previous lines. The script then checks the current position in the dialogue and, for specific lines, switches to an alternate sound effect. For all other lines, the default dialogue sound is played, allowing for variation in audio during key moments.

The script also controls the visibility of the character sprite. Once the dialogue progresses past the first line, the character becomes visible and plays an idle animation. Before that point, the character remains hidden. This helps introduce the character gradually rather than showing them immediately.

he typewriter effect is then triggered to begin displaying the text.The set dialogue text function updates what is shown on screen. It clears the label and applies coloured formatting based on the current speaker, allowing the dialogue to visually distinguish between different characters.

This section handles the typewriter effect and player input. The type_text function gradually displays each line by looping through every character in the full text and adding it one at a time to the visible string. After each character is added, the label is updated and a short delay is applied, creating the typing animation. If typing is interrupted, the function immediately stops and prevents further characters from being added. Once the full line has finished displaying, typing is disabled, the hint becomes visible, and the default dialogue sound stops unless an alternate sound is being used.

The input function allows the player to interact with the dialogue. If the player presses a key or clicks while the text is still typing, the effect is skipped and the full line is instantly shown. If the text has already finished displaying, the input advances the dialogue to the next line.

This function controls how the dialogue progresses. It increases the dialogue index to move to the next line in the sequence. If there are still lines remaining, it calls the function that displays the next piece of dialogue.

Once all dialogue has been completed, both sound effects are stopped and the game transitions to a new scene. This marks the end of the conversation and smoothly moves the player forward into the 3d walking simulator part of the game.
Similarly to The last 2 scenes a stand in photo was used to get a better feel of the game presentation. The background is a photo i took of a building entrance in my area.

Encounter 1 structure draft.The first encounter is inspired by the knife crime chairty people who wait outside the various london stations.

Whenever i have the displeasure of being stopped by someone from the organisation it personally feels like there is a hidden skill check / dialouge check i have to pass to escape the interaction.

The idea behind the card game mini game is based off the pre-talking that they do before they launch into their charity speech. You know theyre wasting your time and they know theyre setting up the stage for the inevitable.

This is where the concept of the rigged card game comes in. It is also an allagory for working class expierence, you get roped into having hope that if you do things 'properly' it will work out. When in reality its rigged against you from the beginning.
Card game layout sketch

This section sets up the structure for a visual novel encounter that has two different phases. The game state controls whether the player is currently seeing the introduction dialogue before the mini-game, or the outro dialogue after the mini-game has finished.

The intro dialogue introduces the strange character and sets up the higher or lower card game encounter. The outro dialogue is used after the mini-game, continuing the scene and wrapping up the interaction. The dialogue index tracks which line is currently being shown, while current dialogue stores whichever dialogue list is active at that moment.

This section controls the setup for the dialogue system. The variables manage the typing effect, including the full line of text, the part currently visible, the text colour, and the speed of the typewriter animation.

When the scene starts, the mouse is made visible, the dialogue box is shown, and the hint is hidden. The script then checks whether the player has just returned from the card game. If they have, it starts the outro dialogue. If not, it starts the intro dialogue. The start_vn function sets the current state, loads the correct dialogue list, resets the dialogue index, and begins showing the first line.

This section handles displaying each line of dialogue and creating the typewriter effect. The function retrieves the current line from the active dialogue list and checks the speaker type to assign a specific text colour, helping distinguish between narration, the player, and the NPC.

It then prepares the text by storing the full line, clearing what is currently visible, and enabling the typing effect. The dialogue label is reset, the hint is hidden, and a prompt is set to indicate how the player can continue. If a sound node is present, the typing sound is restarted for the new line.

The type_text function gradually reveals the dialogue one character at a time, updating the label with coloured text and adding a short delay between each character. If the typing is interrupted, the sound stops and the function exits early. Once the full line has been displayed, typing ends and the hint becomes visible again.

This section manages how the dialogue progresses and how the player interacts with it. The advance function moves to the next line by increasing the dialogue index. If there are still lines remaining, it displays the next one. When all dialogue has been completed, the script stops the sound and transitions to a new scene. If the current state is the intro, the player is sent to the card mini-game. If it is the outro, the game returns to the main scene and updates a global flag to show the encounter has finished

The input function listens for player interaction through a key press or mouse click. If the player presses input while the text is still typing, the typewriter effect is skipped and the full line is instantly displayed. If the text has already finished, the input advances the dialogue to the next line, allowing the player to control the pacing of the conversation.

Initial simple card game layout.Used for debugging and making sure all aspects of the card game functioned correctly. Such as the cards popping up when hovered over, and double checking all input interactions functioned.

3 iterations of the final card game presentation, each with slight visual tweaks. I had initially planned to have the 7 card displayed for clarity (as the player had to pick a random card and guess if its value was higher or lower than 7). In the end this extra visual piece was removed as the stage size was limited and the extra card felt like it was overcrowding the stage. Instead the instructions and dialouge were put in its place.

I used a simple shader as a background because i felt like anything too intricate wouldnt fit and also for simplicity.

This section sets up the card mini-game and prepares all the elements needed for interaction. The script extends a Control node, meaning it manages the user interface for the game. Several UI elements are referenced at the start, including the base card, a set of selectable cards, a reveal card, and a sound effect for hovering.

Variables are used to track the current game state, such as the selected card, the number of losses, and whether the player is waiting to continue. A small set of dialogue lines is also included to respond to repeated losses, adding personality to the encounter.

The ready function initialises the scene by making the mouse visible, enabling formatted text on the result label, and storing the original positions of each card. This allows cards to return to their default position after being hovered over. It also sets up the card visuals, connects button inputs for higher and lower choices, and begins the first round of the game.

This section sets up the game board and prepares each round of the card mini-game. The setup function assigns the base card and sets all selectable cards to show their back, ensuring the player cannot see their values at the start. It also hides the reveal card, which will later display the chosen result.

The connect function links each card to its interactions, allowing the player to click, hover over, and move away from cards. This enables both selection and visual feedback through movement or sound.

The start round function resets the game state for a new turn. It clears any previous selection, updates the instruction text, disables the higher and lower buttons until a card is chosen, and resets all cards to their original positions and appearance.

The card selection function records which card the player chooses and resets the positions of all cards, preparing for the next step of the interaction.

This section handles what happens after the player selects a card. The chosen card is slightly raised to give visual feedback, and the higher and lower buttons are enabled so the player can make their guess. The instruction text is also updated to guide the player on what to do next.

The higher and lower button functions simply pass the player’s choice into the main logic function. The resolve function then processes the outcome. It first checks that a card has been selected, then determines the result using a rigged system and increases the loss counter. The buttons are disabled again and all cards are locked to prevent further input.

Finally, the selected card is revealed by changing its texture, and a line of dialogue is prepared based on how many times the player has lost, adding a narrative response to the outcome.

This section displays the result of the player’s guess. If the result label supports formatted text, the message is shown with coloured styling. It tells the player what they guessed, what card was revealed, and confirms that they lost, followed by a short NPC response. If formatted text is not available, the same information is displayed as plain text.

After the result appears, a continue hint is shown and the game waits for the player to press space. The rigged card function ensures the player always loses by revealing a lower card when they guess higher, or a higher card when they guess lower. The input function then listens for the continue action and moves the game to the next step once the player presses the key.

This function handles the hover effect for the cards. When the player moves the cursor away from a card, it smoothly returns to its original position. The function first checks whether the game is waiting for the player to continue or if the card is currently selected, and if either is true, it prevents any movement.

If the card can be moved, a tween is created to animate the transition back to its original position. This creates a smooth and responsive visual effect, improving the overall feel of interaction with the cards.

This code was used as an early interaction trigger for an encounter scene within the walking simulator section of the project. It is attached to an Area3D node and contains an exported scene path, allowing the target encounter scene to be changed directly from the Inspector without rewriting the script. The script also includes an optional hint path, which can be assigned to a UI prompt and made visible when the scene begins.

During development, the interaction was triggered through the interact input action, which printed a debug message before changing scenes using the SceneTransition system. This made it useful for quickly testing whether encounter transitions were working correctly. However, because the script checks for input every frame rather than confirming whether the player is inside the Area3D, it functions more as a forced interaction test than a final proximity-based trigger. This helped identify the need for more controlled encounter activation later in development.

This part of the code stores the encounter’s dialogue in an array, with each line written as a dictionary containing a type and text. The type identifies whether the line is spoken by the player, the NPC, or used as description, which later allows the script to style or colour the text differently. The dialogue plays in order using dialogue_index, creating a linear visual novel-style conversation. One line also includes 'show_bottle': true, which acts as a trigger to show the bottle image during that moment in the scene.

This section sets up the variables and scene references needed for the dialogue encounter to work. dialogue_index tracks which line is currently being shown, while is_typing, full_text, current_text, current_color, and typing_speed control the typewriter text effect and its appearance. npc_has_left is used later to make sure the NPC stays hidden after walking away. The exported eyes_open and eyes_closed textures allow blinking images to be assigned in the Inspector, while the @onready variables connect the script to important scene nodes such as the portrait, blink timer, and bottle image. In _ready(), the mouse is made visible, the dialogue UI is prepared, the bottle is hidden, the portrait is set to the open-eyes texture, the blink timer is started with a random delay, and the first dialogue line begins.

This function displays the current dialogue line. It gets the line using dialogue_index, then checks the line’s type to choose the correct text colour for description, player, or NPC dialogue. It stores the line’s text in full_text, clears the current text, and turns on is_typing so the typewriter effect can begin. The dialogue label is cleared, the hint is hidden, and the hint text is updated for keyboard/controller input. The function also checks whether the current line has 'show_bottle': true; if so, it shows the bottle image, otherwise it shows the normal portrait. If the NPC has already left, both the portrait and bottle are hidden. Finally, the dialogue sound is restarted so it plays while the new line is being typed.

This section handles special visual events and the typewriter effect. If the current line says He walks away sideways like a crab, the script calls walk_away() to animate the NPC leaving the scene. It then starts type_text(), which gradually displays the dialogue one character at a time. The show_bottle() and hide_bottle() functions control whether the bottle image or NPC portrait is visible. They also check npc_has_left, so once the NPC has walked away, both the portrait and bottle remain hidden. In type_text(), the loop begins typing through full_text, but if typing is interrupted, the dialogue sound stops and the function exits.

This section continues the typewriter effect by adding one character from full_text into current_text, clearing the dialogue label, and then displaying the updated text with the correct colour formatting. The timer creates a short delay between each character, which controls the typing speed. Once the full line has finished typing, is_typing is set to false, the continue hint becomes visible, and the dialogue sound stops. The walk_away() function controls the NPC leaving the scene. It first checks that the portrait is visible, then sets npc_has_left to true so the character stays gone afterwards. A tween is then created to move the portrait sideways while also shifting it slightly up and down, creating the effect of the character walking away sideways.

This section completes the NPC walking animation by adding several delayed tween movements on the portrait’s Y position. The portrait moves slightly up and down while also moving sideways, creating a wobbling motion that makes the exit feel more like a crab walk rather than a simple slide. Each delayed tween changes the vertical position at a different moment, producing a repeated bouncing effect. Once the tween finishes, the callback runs and hides both the portrait and the bottle image, making sure the NPC and prop are no longer visible after the character has left the scene.

This section controls how the player moves through the dialogue and exits the encounter. The advance_dialogue() function increases dialogue_index by one, moving to the next line if there are still lines left in the dialogue array. If the dialogue has finished, it stops the dialogue sound, sets GlobalData.returning_from_encounter to true so the main scene knows the player is returning from an encounter, and then changes back to mainfinal.tscn. The _unhandled_input() function checks whether the player has pressed continue using ui_accept or the left mouse button. If text is still typing, the input skips the typewriter effect and instantly displays the full line, shows the hint, and stops the sound. If the line has already finished, the same input advances to the next dialogue line.

This section controls the blinking animation for the NPC portrait. When the timer finishes, _on_timer_timeout() calls the blink() function. The function first checks that both eye textures exist and that the portrait is currently visible; if not, it stops to prevent errors or blinking while the NPC is hidden. It then briefly changes the portrait texture to the closed-eyes version, waits for 0.1 seconds, and changes it back to the open-eyes version. Finally, the timer is given a new random wait time between 1.5 and 4 seconds before starting again, making the blinking feel more natural instead of happening at fixed intervals.

This script is attached to an Area3D and is used to move the player into encounter_2.tscn. The exported next_scene variable stores the scene path, making it easy to change the target scene from the Inspector. The hint_path variable allows a hint UI element to be assigned, and in _ready() the script checks whether a hint has been provided; if it has, it gets that node and makes it visible. In _process(), the script constantly checks whether the input action interact_a has just been pressed. When it is pressed, the game uses SceneTransition.change_scene(next_scene) to load the encounter scene. This version works as a direct interaction trigger, but it does not check whether the player is inside the Area3D, so pressing the input can activate the transition from anywhere unless additional range-checking logic is added.

This section sets up the dialogue for another visual novel-style encounter. The dialogue array separates narration, NPC speech, and player responses, making it easier to style each type differently. One line includes show_cigs, which is used later to display the cigarette image during the scene.

The remaining variables control the typewriter effect, text colour, and dialogue progress. The NPC sprite and cigarette image are stored so they can be shown or hidden during the encounter.

This section prepares the encounter when the scene starts. It makes the mouse visible, shows the dialogue box, hides the hint and cigarette image, and keeps the NPC sprite visible. It also enables formatted text so the dialogue can use different colours.

The show_dialogue_line function loads the current dialogue line, chooses a colour based on whether it is narration, player dialogue, or NPC speech, then prepares the typewriter effect. It clears the previous text, hides the hint, and updates the continue prompt.

This section checks whether the current dialogue line should display the cigarette image. If show_cigs is active, the cigarette image appears and the NPC sprite is hidden. If not, the cigarette image is hidden and the NPC sprite returns.

The dialogue sound is restarted for each new line, then the typewriter effect begins. The set_dialogue_text function updates the label with the correct colour, while type_text starts revealing the line character by character.

This section continues the typewriter effect by adding each character to the visible text and updating the dialogue label. A short delay between each character creates the typing animation. Once the full line is shown, typing stops, the hint becomes visible, and the dialogue sound is stopped.

The advance_dialogue function moves to the next line. If more dialogue remains, it displays the next line. If the encounter is finished, it stops the sound, marks the player as returning from an encounter, and changes back to the main scene.

This section handles player input during the dialogue. It checks whether the player has pressed the continue button or clicked the mouse. If no valid input is detected, nothing happens.

If the text is still typing, the input skips the typewriter effect and instantly displays the full line. The hint is then shown and the dialogue sound stops. If the line has already finished, the same input advances the dialogue to the next line.

This script controls a 3D encounter trigger area. It extends an Area3D node, meaning it detects when another body, such as the player, enters its space. The exported encounter scene path allows the linked encounter scene to be changed easily in the editor.
The triggered variable prevents the encounter from activating more than once. The arrow is used as a visual indicator to show the player where the encounter is. When the scene starts, the script connects the body entered signal and checks whether this encounter has already been completed. If it has, the arrow is hidden. If not, the arrow remains visible.
When the player enters the area, the script checks that the encounter has not already been triggered or completed. It then hides the arrow, saves the player’s current position and rotation, marks the encounter as completed, and changes to the encounter scene. This allows the game to return the player to the correct location afterwards.

Based on player feedback, I was advised to make the encounter points more noticeable by adding a glow effect and a clearer visual indicator. I tested a few different colours to see which worked best. Blue matched the overall map palette, but blended into the environment too much. Red was very visible, but felt more ominous than intended. I eventually chose yellow, as it stood out clearly while still feeling neutral and approachable.

I also added floating animated arrows above the encounter points to make them easier for players to identify. This gives the player a clearer sense of direction and reduces confusion about where they are supposed to go next. The movement of the arrows helps draw attention without needing extra text instructions, making the encounters feel more naturally integrated into the environment.
Additional red directional arrows were added so that there is obvious indication for players to know where to go.

Another issue I needed to address was directional sensitivity, particularly in relation to the Area3D trigger zones. The player’s turning was initially too broad, which meant that after spawning outside the front door, they could accidentally trigger Encounter 1 simply by turning around. To fix this, I moved the Encounter 1 Area3D trigger box further back and slightly reduced the mouse and controller sensitivity. This made the interaction feel more controlled and helped prevent players from unintentionally activating the encounter.

The poor door entrance uses the same base structure as the nicer main entrance, but it is presented as more neglected and less cared for. This was intentional, as I wanted to highlight how unequal treatment is not always shown through completely separate spaces, but through differences in maintenance, attention, and presentation. By making the poorer entrance feel less polished, the design reflects how working-class residents can be given access that technically functions, but feels secondary, overlooked, or deliberately lower in quality.
Lift background
Lift background reference image

The final lift presentation reinforces the project’s use of frustration and inconvenience. After being redirected through the building and forced to take the longer route, the player finally reaches the lift, only to discover that it is broken. This reflects a familiar lack of care and maintenance in shared housing spaces, where basic access is technically provided but not properly supported. The broken lift becomes a final joke, but also a final criticism: even after following the rules and taking the route assigned to them, the player is still obstructed. It adds to the feeling that the system is not designed with their comfort, time, or access in mind.
